questions.q: Which is an example of an open-ended therapeutic communication technique?
options: 'Tell me more about how you have been feeling this week.'
'Are you feeling sad?'
'You should try to think positively.'
'Everything will be fine, don't worry.'
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions invite the client to elaborate in their own words, encouraging expression of thoughts and feelings rather than a simple yes/no answer.

questions.q: A client reports seeing insects crawling on the wall that are not there. This is an example of:
options: A visual hallucination
A delusion
An illusion
A flight of ideas
questions.explanation: A hallucination is a false sensory perception with no external stimulus (seeing something that isn't there); a delusion, by contrast, is a fixed false belief.

questions.q: A client tells the nurse, 'I don't see the point in going on anymore.' What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Directly and calmly ask the client about thoughts of suicide, and ensure a safe environment
Change the subject to avoid upsetting the client
Assume the comment is attention-seeking and move on
Wait until the next shift to report it
questions.explanation: Any statement suggesting hopelessness should prompt a direct, non-judgemental assessment of suicidal ideation; ensuring immediate safety and reporting are essential priorities in mental health nursing.

questions.q: Maintaining professional boundaries with clients in a psychiatric unit primarily helps to:
options: Protect the therapeutic nature of the nurse-client relationship
Make the nurse's job easier administratively
Reduce documentation requirements
Increase client dependency on the nurse
questions.explanation: Clear professional boundaries protect clients from exploitation and keep the relationship focused on the client's therapeutic needs, rather than the nurse's personal needs.

questions.q: A client on haloperidol develops muscle rigidity, tremors and a shuffling gait. The nurse recognises these as:
options: Extrapyramidal side effects
Signs of improvement
Normal ageing changes
Symptoms of the underlying psychiatric illness only
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol commonly cause extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, akathisia, shuffling gait) due to dopamine blockade in motor pathways, and should be reported for possible dose adjustment or treatment.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes panic disorder from generalised anxiety disorder?
options: Panic disorder involves sudden, intense episodes of fear with physical symptoms, while generalised anxiety disorder involves persistent, excessive worry over time
Generalised anxiety disorder always involves hallucinations
Panic disorder never has physical symptoms
They are the same condition with different names
questions.explanation: Panic disorder is characterised by discrete, sudden panic attacks with intense physical symptoms, whereas generalised anxiety disorder involves chronic, excessive worry about various aspects of life most days over months.

questions.q: Which is a 'negative' symptom of schizophrenia?
options: Flat affect and social withdrawal
Auditory hallucinations
Delusions of persecution
Disorganised speech
questions.explanation: Negative symptoms reflect a loss or reduction of normal function — such as flat affect, social withdrawal and reduced motivation — while positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech) reflect an excess or distortion of normal function.

questions.q: Which finding is a core symptom used to assess major depressive disorder?
options: Persistent low mood and loss of interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)
Excessive energy and euphoria
Rapid, pressured speech
Grandiosity
questions.explanation: Persistent depressed mood and anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure) are core diagnostic features of major depressive disorder, alongside changes in sleep, appetite, energy and concentration.

questions.q: A client with a history of heavy alcohol use is admitted and, 48 hours after their last drink, becomes agitated, tremulous, diaphoretic and starts hallucinating. The nurse should suspect:
options: Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens)
Normal anxiety about hospitalisation
A new psychotic disorder unrelated to alcohol
Simple dehydration
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens typically develops 48-72 hours after the last drink in dependent clients and is a medical emergency marked by autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, confusion and hallucinations, requiring close monitoring and treatment.

questions.q: In mental health nursing, client confidentiality may ethically be broken when:
options: There is a credible, serious risk of harm to the client or an identifiable third party
The client's family simply wants an update
A colleague is curious about the case
The information would make an interesting case study
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is a core ethical principle, but it has recognised limits when a client poses a serious, credible risk of harm to themselves or a specific identifiable other person, in which case safety takes priority.

questions.q: According to crisis intervention theory, a crisis is generally considered self-limiting and resolves, for better or worse, within approximately:
options: 4 to 6 weeks
A few hours
Several years
It never resolves without medication
questions.explanation: Crisis theory holds that a crisis state is time-limited, typically resolving (adaptively or maladaptively) within about four to six weeks as the person's usual coping mechanisms are overwhelmed and then re-stabilise.

questions.q: The core principle of cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) is that:
options: Identifying and restructuring distorted thought patterns can change feelings and behaviour
Unconscious childhood conflicts are the sole focus of treatment
Medication is the only effective intervention
Behaviour cannot be changed through therapy
questions.explanation: CBT is based on the idea that maladaptive thoughts influence emotions and behaviour, so helping clients identify and reframe distorted or unhelpful thinking patterns can produce meaningful change.

questions.q: A client on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) recently started an additional serotonergic medication and now presents with agitation, hyperthermia, tremor and hyperreflexia. The nurse should suspect:
options: Serotonin syndrome
A common cold
Simple dehydration
Normal SSRI onset effects
questions.explanation: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity, often from combining serotonergic drugs, and presents with agitation, hyperthermia, tremor, clonus and hyperreflexia — it requires prompt recognition and intervention as it can be life-threatening.

questions.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops high fever, severe muscle rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability. The nurse's priority is to suspect and report:
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a life-threatening emergency
A mild, expected side effect requiring no action
Normal fever from an unrelated infection only
Improvement in psychiatric symptoms
questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics, marked by hyperthermia, 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental status, requiring immediate medical attention and discontinuation of the causative drug.

questions.q: When de-escalating an agitated client, current evidence-based practice favours which approach first?
options: Calm verbal de-escalation and offering choices in a low-stimulus environment, using restraint only as a last resort
Immediate physical restraint before attempting to speak with the client
Ignoring the client until they calm down alone
Raising one's voice to establish authority
questions.explanation: Least-restrictive, verbal de-escalation techniques — a calm tone, offering choices, reducing environmental stimulation — are recommended first-line approaches; physical or chemical restraint is reserved for situations where safety cannot otherwise be maintained.

questions.q: In therapeutic use of self, 'countertransference' refers to:
options: The nurse's own emotional reactions to the client, often shaped by the nurse's past experiences
The client's feelings toward the nurse based on past relationships
A formal treatment technique used in group therapy
A type of medication side effect
questions.explanation: Countertransference describes the nurse's unconscious emotional responses to a client, which can be shaped by the nurse's own history; recognising it helps the nurse maintain therapeutic objectivity, while transference refers to the client projecting feelings about others onto the nurse.

questions.q: Which factor is most associated with a HIGH level of suicide risk on a nursing assessment?
options: A client who has a specific plan and access to the means to carry it out
A client who denies any thoughts of self-harm and has strong social support
A client with no prior history and vague, fleeting thoughts
A client who is actively engaged in future planning and treatment
questions.explanation: Risk increases substantially when a client has moved from vague ideation to a specific plan combined with access to lethal means; these are core factors nurses assess when determining the urgency of intervention and level of observation needed.

questions.q: What best differentiates hypomania from a full manic episode?
options: Hypomania causes a noticeable change in functioning without severe impairment, psychosis, or need for hospitalisation, unlike mania
Hypomania always requires hospitalisation
Mania is milder and briefer than hypomania
They are clinically identical with no difference
questions.explanation: Hypomania involves a distinct change in mood and energy that is noticeable to others but does not cause marked impairment in functioning, psychotic features, or require hospitalisation — unlike a full manic episode, which does.

questions.q: A general legal/ethical criterion commonly used to justify involuntary psychiatric admission is:
options: The person poses a danger to self or others, or is gravely unable to care for their own basic needs due to mental illness
The person simply disagrees with their family
The person has a low income
The person has previously been hospitalised at any point
questions.explanation: Involuntary admission generally requires evidence that, due to mental illness, the person poses an imminent danger to themselves or others, or is unable to meet basic needs for safety (grave disability) — not merely disagreement with others or past history alone.

questions.q: The recovery model in mental health nursing primarily emphasises:
options: A person-centred approach focused on hope, empowerment and living a meaningful life, not just symptom elimination
Complete symptom elimination as the only measure of success
Lifelong dependence on institutional care
Removing the client's involvement in their own treatment decisions
questions.explanation: The recovery model shifts focus from purely eliminating symptoms toward supporting hope, self-determination and meaningful, self-defined quality of life, with the client as an active partner in their own care.
